corrected.was: fantasy and adventure running longer, sometimes 60,000 to 75,000 or more
corrected.now: fantasy and adventure running longer, sometimes reaching 70,000 or more
corrected.why: The library's own market entry (mkt-len-middle-grade) says 'sometimes reaching 70,000 or more'; no source found supports a 60,000 to 75,000 band, and web sources for middle-grade length vary widely (roughly 20,000 to 65,000 for the category). Now consistent with the library and still hedged.

softened.was: the name is a modern bookselling and library label
softened.now: the name is a bookselling and library label
softened.why: No source dates the label, so 'modern' implied an era that was not established.

softened.was: graphic novels became a large part of the middle-grade market
softened.now: graphic novels became a growing part of the middle-grade market
softened.why: 'Large part' reads as a market-share claim that was not sourced; 'growing' is the defensible general statement. Smile (Graphix, February 2010) confirmed.

softened.was: editors often say it is the first thing they look for in middle grade
softened.now: editors often say it is one of the first things they look for in middle grade
softened.why: A superlative with no basis; softened to a general trade remark.

removed.was: usually explained as coming from American school grades
removed.now: (clause deleted; the point that it is a bookselling and library label, not a literary period, stays)
removed.why: The writer flagged this as the least certain claim. Search found no documented origin of the phrase; one trade article called it an American term tied to the elementary/middle/high school system, but it presents this as plausible, not established. Nothing is said about the origin now.

Word-count ranges (30,000 to 55,000; fantasy reaching 70,000 or more) are trade norms from agent blogs and forums that vary a lot, and now match the library's market entry; they are hedged as rough and publisher-dependent.
Age bands (eight to twelve; lower eight to ten; upper ten to thirteen; tween nine to twelve; picture book usually 32 pages) are trade conventions and carry 'varies'.
'Graphic novels a growing part of the market' and 'Harry Potter showed how large the audience could be' are general, unsourced statements.

softened.was: Eragon (self-published 2002 and reissued by Knopf in 2003)
softened.now: Eragon (first self-published by his family, then reissued by Knopf in 2003)
softened.why: Sources disagree on the year of self-publication (2001 in several bios and one Wikipedia passage, 2002 in the infobox and others). Knopf's edition in 2003 (August) is consistent across sources.
Same dispute; the Knopf year is the safe one and the label says which edition is meant.

softened.was: Secondary-world fantasy with heroines, courts and heists dominated the 2010s
softened.now: Secondary-world fantasy with heroines, courts and heists was a leading strand of the 2010s
softened.why: 'Dominated' is an unsourced market-share claim; 'a leading strand' is defensible.

softened.was: romance-led fantasy (romantasy) and social-media recommendation, notably BookTok, have driven sales
softened.why: Publishers Weekly/BookScan reporting shows BookTok's effect on sales but commentators note other causes (the pandemic reading boom, industry trends); causation is not settled. Date 'since about 2020' is supported (BookTok backlist surges from late 2020).

softened.was: adults read young adult fantasy in large numbers
softened.now: many adults also read young adult fantasy
softened.why: The well-known Bowker study (2012) found 55 percent of buyers of YA books were 18 or older, but it covers YA overall, not fantasy, and buyers are not readers. Softened to a general statement.

softened.was: a single volume of about seventy to a hundred thousand words is typical
softened.now: a single volume of about seventy to a hundred thousand words is a common range
softened.why: Web guidance clusters at about 70,000 to 90,000 with up to 100,000 for fantasy; the library's market entry says fantasy often reaches 100,000 or more. 'Common range' is safer than 'typical'.

softened.was: a label that became common in the early 2020s
softened.now: a label that spread widely in the 2020s
softened.why: The writer flagged this as the least certain date-like claim. Sources say the word was in circulation earlier but became widely recognised around 2023 (Fourth Wing, BookTok). 'Spread widely in the 2020s' is accurate without pinning a year.

'Manic pixie dream girl' is used as a critical label with no attribution (it is generally credited to a film critic in 2007, from memory only; the file makes no coinage claim, so none is needed).

The challenge claim names 'race, sexuality and gender' as themes; the 2010 to 2019 list clearly supports race and sexuality (and sexual content), while gender-themed titles are more prominent in later years' lists. The claim is hedged ('several', 'among those') and was left as written.

Age bands (readers about twelve to eighteen; protagonists about fifteen to eighteen; new adult about eighteen to twenty-five; realistic middle grade about ten to thirteen) are trade conventions marked 'varies'. The library's YA entries use 'fifteen to eighteen' (genre entry) and 'fourteen to eighteen' (YA profile), so the library itself is not uniform.
Word-count range of fifty to ninety thousand matches the library's market entry for YA.
